But in all exchanges a central authority controls and handles the changes.
With the Bitcoin, all network nodes are at the same time bookkeepers, verifiers, issuers of currency and buyers and sellers.
How does that network work?
Each transaction between two users is made in reality between two electronic addresses in the form of email.
A user can choose a different address for each payment, ensuring thus the anonymity.
A set of information related to this transaction is electronically signed through a double-key encryption system.
The network can thus verify the authenticity of the transaction.
Thanks to the content of the file, it is also possible to ensure that the changes of bitcoins are recorded in the public account book, which is spread throughout the network.
The key event consists in writing that new transaction in that book.
This passes through the resolution of a mathematical challenge launched at the computers and the winner, a kind of temporary central banker, will have the privilege of adding that extra line.
It is a phase of file fragmentation, that is, a transformation of a large file into a shorter and unique digital fingerprint.
The computers "take" the new transaction and add a number before "cut" the set.
The goal is to find the number that provides a particular fingerprint (more zeros at the beginning).
Once the number is found, the other nodes verify easily that it is the good one.
The transaction is then inseparably linked to the chain of the other transactions; any modification would change the fingerprint.

If, in order to commit a fraud, a user wanted to pay twice with the same money very quickly (in less than ten minutes), the network would only accept one of the two transactions; the other would remain orphaned, since both have different fingerprints.
The computer that solves the challenge will take 50 bitcoins.
To avoid inflation, that reward is divided into two regularly, with probability before the end of 2012.
The number of bitcoins in circulation is limited to 21 million, but they are divisible up to the hundred millionth, leaving a wide margin.
The difficulty of this challenge is also revealed in each increase of the computing power.

The announcement of the probable discovery of the Higgs boson generated a great shock last summer, and for reason.
It is believed that this boson is a participant in the mechanism responsible for the mass of everything that exists in the universe, nothing more and nothing less.

In this great world, there is a general and inescapable law that implies that two things cannot be found in the same place at the same time.

In this "disorder" a electromagnetic wave (from light, infrared, ultraviolet, etc.) is born, and this wave is not another thing than a photon; that is, one of the bosons "carriers of force".
More stable field
The same happens with the Higgs boson, with the difference that it is another field, the Higgs field, which needs to be "disordered" for this boson to appear.

Bitcoin differs from other virtual currency systems such as "credits", used to advance in a video game and that can be won by playing or can be bought (even in some cases can be exchanged).
The social media Facebook developed this type of system.
But in all exchanges a central authority controls and deals with the changes.
With Bitcoin, all network nodes are at the same time bookkeepers, verifiers, issuers, and buyers and sellers.
How does this network function?
Each transaction between two users is done in reality between two electronic addresses in the form of email.
A user can choose a different address for each payment, ensuring thus anonymity.
A set of information related to this transaction is signed electronically through a double encryption system.
The network can thus verify the authenticity of the transaction.
Thanks to the content of the file, it is also possible to ensure that the changes of bitcoins are recorded in the public account book, which is spread throughout the network.
The key milestone consists in writing this new transaction in that book.
This passes through the resolution of a mathematical challenge launched at the computers and the winner, a kind of provisional central banker, will have the privilege of adding that extra line.
This is a phase of file fragmentation, meaning the transformation of a large file into a shorter and unique numeric trail.
The computers "catch" the new transaction and add a number before "cut" the set.
The goal is to find the number that offers a particular trace (more zeros at the beginning).
Once the number is found, the other nodes verify easily that it is the good one.
The transaction is then inseparably linked to the chain of other transactions; any modification would change the trace.

Yes, in order to commit a fraud, a user would want to pay two times with the same money very quickly (in less than ten minutes), the network would only accept as valid one of the two transactions; the other would be orphaned, since both have different fingerprints.
The computer that solves the challenge will carry 50 bitcoins.
To prevent inflation, that reward is divided into two regularly, with probability before the end of 2012.
The number of bitcoins in circulation is limited to 21 million, but they are divisible up to the 100 millionth, which leaves a wide margin.
The difficulty of this challenge is also revealed in each increase in the power of calculation.

Everything opposite to the current exchange transactions, based on central banks, the identified transactions and the processing charges between the parties.

In fact, Bitcoin, invented by Satoshi Nakamoto (a pseudonym), is at the same time a virtual currency that can be converted to dollars, euros, etc., and a secure protocol in the way of BitTorrent, which allows the exchange of files between equal to equal.
Around 200,000 transactions have been recorded thanks to 15,000 computers in the network.
And near a thousand websites accept bitcoins as donations or as a form of payment.

The price of bitcoin, after reaching a peak of 30 dollars (23 euros) in June 2011, fell to 2 dollars five months later, before returning today to around 10 dollars (the prices are recorded on the bitcoincharts.com page).
It is nothing impressive compared to the changes in real money or financial products.
However, the European Central Bank (BCE) was interested in him in an article published in October about virtual currencies.
In it, the bitcoin was described as "the virtual currency with the most success", "that competes with the dollar or the euro" and "similar to conventional currencies".
Bitcoin differs from other virtual currency systems such as "credits", used to advance in a video game and that can be earned by playing or bought (even in some cases exchanged).
The social media Facebook also developed this type of system.
But in all exchanges a central authority controls and deals with the changes.
With the bitcoin, all the network nodes are at the same time bookkeepers, verifiers, issuers of currency, and buyers and sellers.
How does that network work?
Each transaction between two users is done in reality between two electronic mail addresses.
A user can choose a different address for each payment, ensuring anonymity.
A set of information related to this transaction is electronically signed through a double key encryption system.
The network can thus verify the authenticity of the transaction.
Thanks to the content of the file, it is also possible to ensure that the changes in bitcoins are recorded in the public book of accounts, which is spread over the entire network.
The key milestone consists in writing that new transaction in that book.
This passes through the resolution of a mathematical challenge launched to the computers and the winner, a kind of provisional central banker, will have the privilege of adding that extra line.
This is a phase of file fragmentation, that is, the transformation of a large file into a shorter and unique digital fingerprint.
The computers "catch" the new transaction and add a number before "cutting" the set.
The goal is to find the number that offers a particular fingerprint (more zeros at the beginning).
Once the number is found, the other nodes easily verify that it is the correct one.
The transaction is then inseparably linked to the chain of other transactions; any modification would change the fingerprint.

Yes, in order to commit a fraud, a user would want to pay twice with the same money very quickly (in less than ten minutes), the network would only accept one of the two transactions; the other would remain orphaned, since both have different fingerprints.
The computer that solves the challenge will carry 50 bitcoins.
To avoid inflation, that reward is divided into two regularly, with probability before the end of 2012.
The number of bitcoins in circulation is limited to 21 million, but are divisible up to the hundredthousandth, leaving a wide margin.
The difficulty of this challenge is also revealed in each increase in the power of calculation.

With Bitcoin, pay and sell without banks
Everything opposite to current monetary exchanges, based on central banks, identified transactions and processing charges between the parties.
Moreover, as often happens in technology, the political vision is palpable: the conviction that the current monetary system, composed of banking monopolies, leads to financial crises.

In fact, Bitcoin, invented by Satoshi Nakamoto (a pseudonym), is at the same time a virtual currency that can be converted to dollars, euros, etc. and a secure protocol in the way of BitTorrent, which allows the exchange of files between equal and equal.
More than 200,000 transactions have been recorded thanks to 15,000 computers in the network.
And around a thousand websites accept Bitcoin as donations or as a form of payment.
The price of Bitcoin, after reaching a peak of $30 (23 euros) in June 2011, fell to $2 five months later, before returning today to around $10 (the prices are recorded at the page bitcoincharts.com).
It is nothing impressive when compared with the world's changes in real money or financial products.
However, the European Central Bank (BCE) was interested in him in an report on virtual currencies published in October.
In it, the bitcoin was described as "the virtual currency with most success", "that competes with the dollar or the euro" and "similar to conventional coins".
Bitcoin is different from other virtual currency systems like the "credits" used in a video game and that can be gained by playing or can be bought (even in some cases exchanged).
The social media Facebook also developed this type of system.
But in all exchanges a central authority controls and handles the changes.
With Bitcoin, all the network nodes are at the same time custodians of accounting books, verifiers, currency issuers, and buyers and sellers.
How does this network function?
Each transaction between two users is done in reality between two electronic addresses in the form of email.
A user can choose a different address for each payment, ensuring thus the anonymity.
A set of information related to this transaction is signed electronically through a double-key encryption system.
The network can thus verify the authenticity of the transaction.
Thanks to the content of the file, it is also possible to ensure that the changes of bitcoins are recorded in the public account book, which is spread throughout the network.
The key event consists in writing this new transaction in this book.
This passes through the solution of a mathematical challenge launched at the computers and the winner, a kind of temporary central bank, will have the privilege of adding that extra line.
This is a phase of file fragmentation, i.e., a transformation of a large file into a shorter and unique digital fingerprint.
The computers "take" the new transaction and add a number before "split" the set.
The goal is to find the number that provides a particular fingerprint (more zeros at the beginning).
Once the number is found, the other nodes verify easily that it is the good one.
The transaction is then inseparably linked to the chain of other transactions; any modification would change the trace.

Yes, in order to commit a fraud, a user would want to pay twice with the same money very quickly (within less than ten minutes), the network would only accept one of the two transactions; the other would be left orphaned, since both have different fingerprints.
The computer that solves the challenge will take 50 bitcoins.
In order to prevent inflation, that reward is divided into two regularly, with probability before the end of 2012.
The number of bitcoins in circulation is limited to 21 million, but they are divisible to the hundred-millionth, which leaves a wide margin.
The difficulty of this challenge is also revealed in each increase in the power of calculation.
The life of the network has already its ups and downs.
The websites that offer services for Bitcoin have been attacked and bitcoins have been stolen from deposit.
"The decision made does not affect the same protocol", says Pierre Noizat, who just launched Paymium, a real money payment company that uses the Bitcoin network.
The ECB also takes account of the possibilities of money laundering through this anonymous service.
But the cash presents the same defect.
The heavy actors, like Wikipedia, reject these payments.
Others, like the Wordpress platform, they accept.
Recently, Adi Shamir and Dorit Ron, from the Weizmann Institute in Israel, analyzed the accounting book and showed that more than 80% of bitcoins are not circulating.
In November, the "big sales" were launched.
"They changed 30,000 dollars", joyfully says Jon Holmquist, who works for Coinabul, which converts bitcoins into gold.
Pierre Noizat, author of a pedagogical book on that coin, believes quite a bit in the potential of this technology as well as in the transaction network.

Each transaction between two users is made in reality between two electronic addresses in the form of e-mail.

More than 200,000 transactions have been recorded thanks to 15,000 computers on the network.

However, the European Central Bank (BCE) was interested in him in an report on virtual currencies published in October.

Facebook, the social network, also developed this type of system.
But in all exchanges a central authority controls and deals with the changes.
With Bitcoin, all network nodes are at the same time accountants, verifiers, issuers of currency, buyers and sellers.
How does this network work?
Each transaction between two users is made in reality between two electronic addresses in the form of email.
A user can choose a different address for each payment, ensuring anonymity.
A set of information related to this transaction is signed electronically through a double-key encryption system.
The network can thus verify the authenticity of the transaction.
Thanks to the content of the file, it is also possible to ensure that the changes in bitcoins are recorded in the public accounts book, which is spread throughout the network.
The key event consists in writing that new transaction in that book.
This passes through the resolution of a mathematical challenge launched at the computers and the winner, a kind of temporary central bank, will have the privilege of adding that additional line.
This is a phase of file fragmentation, that is, a transformation of a large file into a shorter and unique digital fingerprint.
The computers "capture" the new transaction and add a number before "cutting" the set.
The goal is to find the number that offers a particular fingerprint (more zeros at the beginning).
Once the number is found, the other nodes quickly verify that it is the correct one.
The transaction is then inseparable from the chain of other transactions; any modification would change the signature.

Yes, to commit fraud, a user would want to pay twice with the same money very quickly (in less than ten minutes), the network would only accept one of the two transactions; the other would remain orphaned, since both have different fingerprints.
The computer that solves the challenge will carry 50 bitcoins.
To prevent inflation, that reward is divided into two regularly, with probability before the end of 2012.
The number of bitcoins in circulation is limited to 21 million, but they are divisible up to the hundredth millionth, leaving a wide margin.
The difficulty of this challenge is revealed also in each increase in computing power.

Over 200,000 transactions have been recorded thanks to 15,000 computers in the network.

The Bitcoin price, after reaching a peak of $30 (23 euros) in June 2011, fell to $2 five months later, before returning today to around $10 (the prices are listed on the page bitcoincharts.com).
It's nothing impressive compared to the changes in real currency or financial products.
However, the European Central Bank (BCE) was interested in him in a report on virtual currencies published in October.
In it, Bitcoin was described as "the virtual currency with the most success", "that competes with the dollar or the euro" and "similar to conventional currencies".
Bitcoin is different from other virtual currency systems such as "credits", used to advance in a video game and that can be earned by playing or bought (and even in some cases exchanged).
The social network Facebook developed also this type of system.
But in all exchanges a central authority controls and handles the changes.
With Bitcoin, all network nodes are at the same time bookkeepers, verifiers, currency issuers, and buyers and sellers.
How does that network work?
Each transaction between two users is made in reality between two electronic mail addresses.
A user can choose a different address for each payment, ensuring anonymity.
A set of information related to this transaction is signed electronically through a double encryption system.
The network can thus verify the authenticity of the transaction.
Thanks to the content of the file, it is also possible to ensure that the changes in Bitcoin are recorded in the public account, which is spread throughout the network.
The key event consists in writing that new transaction in that book.
This passes through the resolution of a mathematical challenge launched at computers and the winner, a kind of temporary central bank, will have the privilege of adding that extra line.
This is a phase of file fragmentation, that is, a transformation of a large file into a shorter and unique digital signature.
The computers " catch" the new transaction and add a number before " to cut" the set.
The goal is to find the number that provides a unique fingerprint (more zeros at the beginning).
Once that number is found, the rest of the nodes verify easily that it is the good one.
The transaction is then inseparable from the chain of other transactions; any change would change the trace.

Yes, in order to commit a fraud, a user would want to pay twice with the same money very quickly (in less than ten minutes), the network would only accept as valid one of the two transactions; the other would remain orphaned, since both have different fingerprints.
The computer that solves the challenge will carry 50 bitcoins.
To avoid inflation, that reward is divided into two regularly, with probability before the end of 2012.
The number of bitcoins in circulation is limited to 21 million, but they are divisible up to the 100,000th, leaving a wide margin.
The difficulty of this challenge is also shown in each increase in computing power.
The life of the network has already its ups and downs.

With Bitcoin, all the network nodes are at the same time bookkeepers, verifiers, currency issuers, and buyers and sellers.
How does that network work?
Each transaction between two users is made in reality between two electronic addresses in the form of email.
A user can choose a different address for each payment, ensuring anonymity.
A set of information related to this transaction is signed electronically through a double-key encryption system.
The network can thus verify the authenticity of the transaction.
Thanks to the content of the file, it is also possible to ensure that the changes in bitcoins are recorded in the public book of accounts, which is spread throughout the network.
The key event consists in writing that new transaction in that book.
This passes through the solution of a mathematical challenge launched to the computers and the winner, a kind of temporary central banker, will have the privilege of adding that extra line.
This is a phase of file fragmentation, that is, a transformation of a large file into a shorter and unique digital signature.
The computers "take" the new transaction and add a number before "cutting" the set.
The goal is to find the number that offers a particular fingerprint (more zeros at the beginning).
Once the number is found, the other nodes verify easily that it is the good one.
The transaction is then inseparably linked to the chain of other transactions; any modification would change the fingerprint.

Yes, in order to commit a fraud, a user would want to pay twice with the same money very quickly (within less than ten minutes), the network would only accept one of the two transactions; the other would be orphaned, since both have different fingerprints.
The computer that solves the challenge will be given 50 bitcoins.
To avoid inflation, that reward is divided into two regularly, with probability before the end of 2012.

The announcement of the probable discovery of the Higgs boson generated a great shock last summer, and for reason.
It is believed that this boson is a participant in the mechanism responsible for the mass of everything that exists in the universe, nothing more and nothing less.
And what is more, it is the particle whose existence the standard model predicted: our best or "less bad" explanation of the nature and behavior of matter, which has yet to be observed empirically.
But for the physicists it is not completely clear that it is the Higgs.
We certainly know that there is a new particle and that it resembles much the Higgs boson predicted by the standard model.

In this great world, there is a generalized and ineludible law that implies that two things cannot be found in the same place at the same time.
There is no way to violate that rule and don't try too hard, because it will end up hurting yourself.

The physicists classify the particles into two categories.

According to the Particle Adventure page of the Berkeley Laboratories, which is extraordinary, the bosons are divided into two groups: the mesons, of which we will not talk here, and the "force particles", by which the great forces of nature propagate and with which the Higgs boson would be related in some way
It is important to note here that these bosons are not the exotic creatures that we might believe.
In fact, if he manages to read this article, it is thanks to an extraordinary, banal particle: the photon or the "light particle" that acts as the "message" of the electromagnetic force.
In fact, when a charged particle accelerates or changes direction, it "disorders" the electromagnetic field in that very environment; a little like when we throw a stone into a pond.
In this "disorder" a electromagnetic wave (of light, infrared, ultraviolet, etc.) is born, and this wave is not another thing than a photon; that is, one of the "force carriers" of the bosons.
Most stable field
The same happens with the Higgs boson, with the difference that it is another field, the Higgs field, which needs to be "disordered" for this boson to appear.

Now, the Higgs field is much more stable than the electromagnetic field. To activate it, one needs to reach extremely high energies, a little like if it were a frozen lake in which only a heavy rock could slide across the surface.
Therefore, a huge particle accelerator like the one at CERN (the great hadron collider is an 27 km ring!) is needed to reach such levels of energy.

Every transaction between two users is made in reality between two electronic addresses in the form of email.

The computers "take" the new transaction and add a number before "cutting" the set.
The goal is to find the number that offers a particular fingerprint (more zeros at the beginning).
Once that number is found, the other nodes verify easily that it is the good one.
The transaction is then indestructibly linked to the chain of other transactions; any modification would change the fingerprint.

Yes, in order to commit a fraud, a user would want to pay twice with the same money very quickly (in less than ten minutes), the network would only accept as valid one of the two transactions; the other would remain orphaned, since both have different fingerprints.

In fact, Bitcoin, created by Satoshi Nakamoto (a pseudonym), is at the same time a virtual currency that can be converted to dollars, euros, etc., and a secure protocol in the way of BitTorrent, which allows the exchange of files between equal to equal.
Over 200,000 transactions have been recorded thanks to 15,000 computers in the network.
And near a thousand websites accept Bitcoin as donations or as a form of payment.
The price of Bitcoin, after reaching a peak of $30 (€23) in June 2011, fell to $2 five months later, before returning today to around $10 (the prices are listed on the Bitcoincharts.com page).
It is nothing remarkable when compared with the changes in real money or financial products.
However, the European Central Bank (BCE) was interested in him in an October report on virtual currencies.
In it, the bitcoin was described as "the virtual currency with the most success", "which competes with the dollar or the euro" and "similar to the traditional coins".
Bitcoin differs from other virtual currency systems such as the "credits" used to advance in a video game and that can be earned by playing or bought (even in some cases exchanged).
The social network Facebook also developed this type of system.
But in all exchanges a central authority controls and handles the changes.
With Bitcoin, all the network nodes are at the same time bookkeepers, verifiers, issuers of currency, and buyers and sellers.
How does that network work?
Each transaction between two users is carried out in reality between two electronic addresses in the form of email.
A user can choose a different address for each payment, ensuring anonymity.
A set of information related to this transaction is signed electronically through a double-key encryption system.
The network can thus verify the authenticity of the transaction.
Thanks to the content of the file, it is also possible to ensure that the changes in bitcoins are recorded in the public accounts book, which is spread throughout the network.
The key event consists in writing that new transaction in that book.
This passes through the resolution of a mathematical challenge launched at the computers and the winner, a kind of temporary central banker, will have the privilege of adding that extra line.
This is a phase of file fragmentation, that is, the transformation of a large file into a shorter and unique digital fingerprint.
The computers "catch" the new transaction and add a number before "cutting" the set.
The goal is to find the number that provides a particular fingerprint (more zeros at the beginning).
Once the number is found, the other nodes verify easily that it is the good one.
The transaction is then inseparably linked to the chain of other transactions; any modification would change the trace.

Yes, in order to commit a fraud, a user would want to pay twice with the same money very quickly (in less than ten minutes), the network would only accept as valid one of the two transactions; the other would be orphaned, since both have different fingerprints.
The computer that solves the challenge will carry 50 bitcoins.
To avoid inflation, that reward is divided into two regularly, with probability before the end of 2012.
The number of bitcoins in circulation is limited to 21 million, but they are divisible up to the hundred-millionth, leaving a wide margin.
The difficulty of this challenge is also shown in each increase in the computing power.
The life of the network has already its ups and downs.
The websites that offer services for Bitcoin have been attacked and bitcoins have been stolen from the deposit.
"The decision made does not affect the same protocol," says Pierre Noizat, who just launched Paymium, a real currency payment company that uses the Bitcoin network.
The ECB also takes into account the possibilities of money laundering through this anonymous service.
But the cash money has the same defect.
The heavy actors, such as Wikipedia, reject these payments.
Others, such as the WordPress platform, are also accepted.
Recently, Adi Shamir and Dorit Ron, from the Weizmann Institute in Israel, analyzed the accounting book and showed that nearly 80% of bitcoins are not circulating.
In November, the "big sales" were launched.
"They changed 30,000 dollars," Jon Holmquist, who works for Coinabul, who converts bitcoins into gold, is elated.
Pierre Noizat, author of a pedagogical book on that currency, believes quite a bit in the potential of this technology as well as in the network of transactions.
His system, Paytunia, is equivalent to a credit card (in real) or a mobile payment without contact, but uses Bitcoin to validate the transactions, which thus become cheaper.
The carrier, in addition, manages their identity and can therefore remain in the anonymity.
The system is easy to set up in the shops, which do not need to install new terminals or software.
Pierre Noizat says that the users are millions, and that the system is ready to be used by anyone with a phone that can "take a photo and recognize it".
There is a general movement for revision of the hierarchical systems to more horizontal systems.
"It will take time for Bitcoin to be accepted, but in 2013 there could be a change," predicts.
On the other hand, in his report the ECB will re-evaluate the various risks, which are currently considered high, in the event that this currency succeeds.

With Bitcoin, all the network nodes are at the same time bookkeepers, verifiers, issuers of currency, and buyers and sellers.

Each transaction between two users is made in reality between two electronic mail addresses.
A user can choose a different address for each payment, ensuring anonymity.
A set of information related to this transaction is signed electronically through a double-key encryption system.
The network can thus verify the authenticity of the transaction.
Thanks to the content of the file, it is also possible to ensure that the changes in Bitcoin are recorded in the public account book, which is spread throughout the network.
The key event consists in writing that new transaction in that book.
This passes through the resolution of a mathematical challenge launched at the computers and the winner, a kind of provisional central banker, will have the privilege of adding that extra line.
This is a phase of file fragmentation, that is, the transformation of a large file into a shorter and unique digital fingerprint.
The computers "catch" the new transaction and add a number before "cutting" the set.
The goal is to find the number that offers a particular fingerprint (more zeros at the beginning).
Once the number is found, the other nodes verify easily that it is the good one.
The transaction is then inseparably linked to the chain of the other transactions; any modification would change the fingerprint.

Yes, in order to commit a fraud, a user would want to pay twice with the same money very quickly (in less than ten minutes), the network would only accept as valid one of the two transactions; the other would remain orphaned, since both have different fingerprints.
The computer that solves the challenge will take 50 bitcoins.

Since 2011, a dozen of states has adopted laws that require voters to show that they are American citizens.
Those measures are intended to, clearly, limit the Hispanic vote.
It seems that two out of three Hispanic voters support the Democratic Party.
On the other hand, the Republican legislators supported in 2011 certain laws that abolished the registration of voters on the same day as the vote in eight states.
In addition, they limited the right of people and groups to create an assistance service for voters who wished to register.
These restrictions have consequences.
For example, in the 2004 general elections, the voter registration campaigns contributed to the registration of around 10 million citizens.
The measures taken since 2009 have resulted in the number of new voters registered in 2010 being lower than in 2006.
In addition, the Republican legislators passed laws in five other states that favored the reduction of the voting period in advance.
For example, in the 2008 elections in Florida, 33% of the voters who voted early were African American, while these latter were only 13% of the state's voters.
In the case of Hispanics, it happened exactly the same.
These represent no more than 11% of the voters, which is equivalent to 24% of the citizens who vote in advance.
However, the whites, who represent 76% of the electorate, do not represent more than 46% of the voters who vote in advance.
Naturally, the Democratic legislators and their supporters have opposed the adoption of laws that restrict the registration of voters.
In this regard, the Democratic governors have blocked several pieces of legislation.
The United States Attorney General intervened to suspend the most controversial laws.
It was, in part, possible to limit the damage.
For example, only 16 of 34 states have adopted the law requiring the presentation of an identification document with a photograph.
However, it is undeniable that the new rules adopted will complicate the exercise of the right to vote in 2012.
The Democratic critics denounce the partisan character of the laws that have been voted, since it is clear that with them, the results of 2012 in the key states are to be influenced.
A 2011 report by the Brennan Center shows that the states that have adopted these laws account for 171 of the 270 votes needed in the electoral college to win the presidency.
It is too early to state with certainty whether these legislative changes at the level of the electoral system will have a significant impact on the results of the 2012 presidential elections.
One thing is certain: those new provisions will negatively affect the participation rate.
In this sense, the measures will damage part of the American democratic system.

With Bitcoin, pay and sell without banks
Everything contrary to the current exchange rates, based on central banks, the identified transactions and the processing charges between the parties.
In addition, as is often the case with technologies, the political vision is palpable: the conviction that the current monetary system, composed of banking monopolies, leads to financial crises.

In fact, Bitcoin, created by Satoshi Nakamoto (a pseudonym), is at the same time a virtual currency that can be converted to dollars, euros, etc., and a secure protocol in the way of BitTorrent, which allows the exchange of files between equal to each other.
Over 200,000 transactions have been recorded thanks to 15,000 computers in the network.
And near a thousand websites accept Bitcoin as donations or as a form of payment.
The price of Bitcoin, after reaching a peak of $30 (23 euros) in June 2011, fell to $2 five months later, before returning to around $10 today (prices are quoted on the page bitcoincharts.com).
It is nothing remarkable when compared to the changes in currency or financial products worldwide.
However, the European Central Bank (BCE) was interested in him in an report on virtual currencies published in October.
In it, the bitcoin was described as "the most successful virtual currency", "which competes with the dollar or the euro" and "similar to the traditional coins".
Bitcoin differs from other virtual currency systems such as the "credits", used to advance in a video game and that can be earned by playing or bought (even in some cases exchanged).
The social network Facebook also developed this type of system.
But in all exchanges a central authority controls and handles the changes.
With Bitcoin, all network nodes are at the same time bookkeepers, verifiers, issuers of currency, and buyers and sellers.
How does that network work?
Each transaction between two users is carried out in reality between two electronic addresses in the form of email.
A user can choose a different address for each payment, ensuring anonymity.
A set of information related to this transaction is signed electronically through a double-key encryption system.
The network can thus verify the authenticity of the transaction.
Thanks to the content of the file, it is also possible to ensure that the changes in bitcoins are recorded in the public account book, which is spread throughout the network.
The key event consists in writing that new transaction in that book.
This passes through the resolution of a mathematical challenge launched at the computers and the winner, a kind of temporary central banker, will have the privilege of adding that additional line.
This is a phase of file fragmentation, that is, the transformation of a large file into a shorter and unique digital fingerprint.
The computers "catch" the new transaction and add a number before "cut" the set.
The goal is to find the number that provides a unique fingerprint (more zeros at the beginning).
Once the number is found, the other nodes verify quickly that it is the correct one.
The transaction is then inseparably linked to the chain of other transactions; any modification would change the fingerprint.

Yes, in order to commit a fraud, a user would want to pay twice with the same money very quickly (in less than ten minutes), the network would only accept as valid one of the two transactions; the other would remain orphaned, since both have different fingerprints.
The computer that solves the challenge will carry 50 bitcoins.
To prevent inflation, that reward is divided into two regularly, with probability before the end of 2012.

It is nothing impressive when compared with the changes in real money or financial products.
However, the European Central Bank (BCE) was interested in him in an October report on virtual currencies.
In it, the bitcoin was described as "the virtual currency with the most success", "that competes with the dollar or the euro" and "similar to conventional currencies".
Bitcoin differs from other virtual currency systems such as the "credits", used to advance in a video game and that can be earned by playing or bought (even in some cases exchanged).
The social network Facebook also developed this type of system.
But in all exchanges a central authority controls and handles the changes.
With Bitcoin, all the network nodes are at the same time bookkeepers, verifiers, issuers of currency, and buyers and sellers.
How does that network work?
Each transaction between two users is made in reality between two electronic mail addresses.
A user can choose a different address for each payment, ensuring anonymity.
A set of information related to this transaction is signed electronically through a double-key encryption system.
The network can thus verify the authenticity of the transaction.
Thanks to the content of the file, it is also possible to ensure that the changes in bitcoins are recorded in the public account book, which is spread throughout the network.
The key event consists in writing that new transaction in that book.
This passes through the resolution of a mathematical challenge launched at the computers and the winner, a kind of temporary central banker, will have the privilege of adding that extra line.
This is a phase of file fragmentation, that is, the transformation of a large file into a shorter and unique digital fingerprint.
The computers "catch" the new transaction and add a number before "cutting" the set.
The goal is to find the number that offers a particular fingerprint (more zeros at the beginning).
Once that number is found, the other nodes verify easily that it is the good one.
The transaction is then inseparably linked to the chain of other transactions; any modification would change the fingerprint.

Yes, in order to commit a fraud, a user would want to pay twice with the same money very quickly (in less than ten minutes), the network would only accept as valid one of the two transactions; the other would remain orphaned, since both have different fingerprints.
The computer that solves the challenge will carry 50 bitcoins.
To avoid inflation, that reward is divided into two regularly, with probability before the end of 2012.
The number of bitcoins in circulation is limited to 21 million, but they are divisible up to the hundred-millionth, leaving a wide margin.
The difficulty of this challenge is also revealed in each increase in the computing power.

It is a new double or nothing with the President Mohammed Morsi.

The surprise of the Wednesday when he announced that the Constituent Assembly would vote his final text the next day.
Just a week ago, the Head of State had given two more months to this Assembly to finish its work.
And almost two years have passed since Egypt has used a provisional text, several times revised, which weakens the institutional stability and leads to judicial entanglements.
This new initiative has only increased the fracture in the country.
For his opponents, the president persists in his "autocratic delirium" and continues "betraying his word" and "stepping on the right".
On the part of its supporters, it is assured that this is a measure to end the institutional and political crisis more quickly and to accelerate the transition process.
In the next 15 days, a referendum should be organized.
A very short time that forces the Brothers to resign from their project of explaining the text, article by article, to the Egyptians.
For the president, it is also a form of restoring popular and democratic legitimacy while the controversy is causing havoc throughout the country.
Mohammed Morsi seems convinced that the Egyptians will vote for him, as he stated in an interview with the American weekly magazine Time.

Considering that this resource has been voted on with great speed, it contains an ultimatum for the Egyptian people: "Vote my text or I will keep the full powers", powers that supposedly will end with the adoption of the Constitution.
It was in this strange atmosphere in which 85 members of this Constituent Assembly, mostly Muslim, voted the text yesterday.
Most of the liberals did not attend the call.
In mid-November, a little before the constitutional declaration, they had closed the door because they thought they could not make their views prevail.
The representatives of human rights, religious minorities, and civil society made the same.
In order to achieve the necessary quorum, 11 substitute members were added hastily this morning.
Some of them are very close to the Muslim Brothers.
As expected, the articles passed unanimously.

The text, which was still being voted on yesterday afternoon, consists of 234 articles.
Article 2, the subject of all eyes, is finally identical to the one in the 1971 Constitution, which stipulated that "the principles of Sharia constitute the main source of law."

The Salafist parties, for whom the establishment of Islamic law is a fundamental claim, hoped that they could replace "the principles" with "the rules", which would have allowed a more strict application.
For the Islamic group, that this article has not been modified is a guarantee of their good will and respect for the other components of Egyptian society.
The liberals call him hypocrisy and consider that it is not more than a publicity stunt.
